newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 21.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- GEORGE REPEATS CALL FOR INTEREST RATE RISE

The debate between chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George over interest rates has flared up again, with George insisting that the base rate has to rise again soon. His comments, made in a speech to bankers in Edinburgh, follow a meeting with Clarke last week at which the chancellor decided to keep interest rates at their current level. George's comments suggest that the issue is likely to remain public in the run up to the general election.
-- LANG SIGNALS COMPETITION POLICY U-TURN

Trade Secretary Ian Lang is expected Tuesday to respond to a report on Britain's competition policy which brands the current system as "weak and confusing". The report has been prepared by the Commission on Public Policy and British Business, a group which includes the heads of some of the UK's largest companies. Lang is likely to reveal that the government is considering making it illegal for companies to abuse their market power, one of the main recommendations of the report.
-- LLOYD'S PLANS CLOSE CHECK ON UNDERWRITER DEALING

Lloyd's of London, the insurance market, is considering installing an electronic system to monitor closely the business activities of underwriters on its insurance syndicates. The move, which could happen later this year, is part of efforts by Lloyd's to prevent a recurrence of the heavy losses which almost destroyed the market. Some underwriters have expressed concern at news of the proposals.
-- STAMP PRICES TO BE FROZEN FOR 15 MONTHS

The Post Office has announced that the price of stamps is to be frozen for at least 15 months. The move, which follows a record Christmas and a speedy recovery from industrial action last year, means the prices for first-class postage will have been running at 14 percent below inflation over the last 15 years. The Post Office also said it is aiming to cut 100 million sterling from central overheads over the next few years, including some job losses.
-- JUMP IN PRICES OF HOMES "COULD FORCE RATE RISE"

Britain's estate agency industry has warned that interest rates will have to rise if the current rate of increase in home prices continues. A survey of more than 250 estate agents in England and Wales, published by the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, found that 89 percent of agents expect prices to rise faster than inflation in 1997. The report concluded that "further interest rate rises and the abolition of Miras (mortgage income tax relief at source) look increasingly likely".
-- CAR OUTPUT HITS POST-1973 HIGH

Figures from the Office for National Statistics reveal that car production in the UK last year totalled 1.69 million units, a rise of 10 percent on the previous year and the highest level since 1973. Output of cars for export rose almost 22 percent, to 908,212 units, while production of commercial vehicles for export also increased by almost 22 percent, to 112,487 vehicles. Overall UK production of commercial vehicles was 238,268, an increase of 2.3 percent.
-- THORN SHARES TUMBLE ON WARNING

Rentals group Thorn has issued a profits warning, prompting a fall of 17 percent in the share price of the group. Thorn said that profits are not expected to rise above last year's 170.7 million stg. Announcing the trading statement, Thorn's chief executive Mike Metcalf said that shareholders have a right to be angry over the performance. He blamed tough trading in the US, mistakes in the UK and adverse exchange rate movements for the performance.
-- OLIVETTI AGREES TO SELL PC BUSINESS

Troubled Italian information technology group Olivetti has agreed to sell its loss-making personal-computer business for a total of between L250bn and L300bn (96 million stg and 116 million stg). The sale leaves Olivetti free to concentrate on telecommunications. The buyer is Piedmont International, a private company set up specially for the deal by Edward Gottesman, a London-based lawyer behind the Centenary industrial holding company.
-- EUROTUNNEL TO ASK FOR FURTHER DEBT STANDSTILL

Channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel has called for a further nine-month extension of its interest payment moratorium. The call was made to the Anglo-French group's 225 banks, which are owed a total of 8.7 billion stg. Eurotunnel, which suffered a fire in one of its tunnels last November, has not paid interest on its debt since September 1995. It has also announced a postponement, from April until June, of a shareholder meeting called to approve last year's 4.7 billion stg debt restructuring plan.
-- PHARMACIA & UPJOHN CHIEF EXECUTIVE QUITS

John Zabriskie has resigned suddenly as chairman of Pharmacia & Upjohn, the Swedish-US drugs group which has its headquarters at Windsor, west of London. The shock departure prompted a slide in the company's share price as investors feared the resignation could presage bad news on the company's performance. P&U have said the departure was not linked to any problems over financial performance or to any differences in strategy.
